The title held by the first governor‑general of India was simply **“Governor‑General of India.”**  
William Cavendish‑Bentinck was the inaugural holder of that office, serving from 22 April 1834 to 20 March 1835, when it was established as the head of the British administration over the entire territory controlled by the East India Company (later the Crown) [1].  

**Position:** Governor‑General of India (the British crown’s chief representative and head of the colonial government in India).

[Lieutenant-General] "Lieutenant-general (United Kingdom)")**Lord William Henry Cavendish-Bentinck** (14 September 1774–17 June 1839) better known as **Lord William Bentinck**, was a British military commander and colonial administrator, who served as the first [governor-general of India] from 1828 to 1835.

He was [Governor of Madras] from 1803 to 1807, but was recalled when his tactless orders on military dress caused a mutiny. As commander of British troops in Sicily and later Naples and [Genoa], he worked against the policy of the London government to encourage self-rule in Sicily and later further north in Italy. His policies were thwarted by London, and to some extent Italian lack of enthusiasm, and he was eventually recalled.

After several years in Parliament in London, he was again sent to India, as the first governor general of all the [East India Company]'s domains. He has been credited for significant social and educational reforms in India, including abolishing [sati] "Sati (practice)"), forbidding women to witness the cremations on the [ghats] of [Varanasi],[[1]] and suppressing [female infanticide] and [human sacrifice].[[2]]

Bentinck noted "the dreadful responsibility hanging over his head in this world and the next, if… he was to consent to the continuance of this practice (sati) one moment longer." After consultation with the army and officials, he passed the [Bengal Sati Regulation, 1829].[[3]] This was challenged by the [Dharma Sabha] which appealed in the [Privy Council]; however, the ban on sati was upheld.[[4]]

He has been credited with reducing lawlessness by eliminating the supposed [Thuggee] with the aid of his chief captain, [William Henry Sleeman]. Along with [Thomas Babington Macaulay] he introduced English as the language of instruction in India.[[5]][[6]][[7]][[8]]

[Mysore] was [annexed] under his presidency.[[9]][[10]]

## Background

[[edit]]

[![Image 5]].jpg)

Portrait by [Thomas Lawrence], 1804

Bentinck was born in Buckinghamshire, the second son of Prime Minister [William Bentinck, 3rd Duke of Portland], and [Lady Dorothy] (née Cavendish), only daughter of [William Cavendish, 4th Duke of Devonshire]. On the marriage the family name became _Cavendish-Bentinck_.[[11]]

He was educated at [Westminster School], a boys' [public school] "Public school (United Kingdom)") in [Westminster, London].[[12]]

## Early career

[[edit]]

In 1783, at the age of 9, he was given the sinecure of [Clerk of the Pipe] for life.[[13]]

Bentinck joined the [Coldstream Guards] on 28 January 1791 at the age of 16, purchasing an ensign's commission.[[14]] He was promoted to captain-lieutenant (lieutenant) in the [2nd Regiment of Dragoons] on 4 August 1792,[[15]] and to captain in the [11th Regiment of Light Dragoons] on 6 April 1793.[[16]] He was promoted to major in the 28th Foot on 29 March 1794[[17]] and to lieutenant-colonel in the [24th Dragoons] that July.[[18]] On 9 January 1798, Bentinck was promoted to colonel.[[19]] In 1803 he was, to some surprise, appointed [Governor of Madras], and was promoted to [major-general] on 1 January 1805.[[20]] Although his tenure was moderately successful, it was brought to an end by the [Vellore Mutiny] in 1806, prompted by Bentinck's order that the native troops be forbidden to wear their traditional attire. Only after serious violence was order restored and the offending policy rescinded, and Bentinck was recalled in 1807.
